subject: anatomy
title: Soleus Muscle (Peripheral Heart), Ankle Ligaments, and Tarsal Tunnel

steps.tx: Within the deep substance of the soleus muscle lie extensive valved sinusoidal venous plexuses. Intermittent rhythmic contraction of soleus during walking compresses these intramuscular sinuses, forcefully pumping venous blood upward against gravity into the popliteal vein, earning the soleus its physiological title as the **peripheral heart** of the circulation.
steps.say: Large venous sinuses reside within the soleus muscle. Rhythmic contraction during walking squeezes these sinuses, propelling blood toward the heart and earning soleus the title of the peripheral heart.

nodes.label: Soleal Venous Sinusoids Fill during Muscular Relaxation
Competent Venous Valves Direct Blood Cephalad
Prevents Dependent Venous Stasis and Deep Vein Thrombosis

steps.tx: The talocrural articulation (ankle joint) is a synovial hinge joint formed between the deep mortise of the distal tibia and fibula and the trochlea of the talus. It permits only **plantarflexion and dorsiflexion**, with greater bony stability in full dorsiflexion because the anterior part of the talar trochlea is wider than the posterior part.
steps.say: The ankle joint is a synovial hinge joint formed by the tibial-fibular mortise and the talar trochlea. It allows only dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, achieving maximal stability in dorsiflexion because the talus is wider anteriorly.

left.title: Dorsiflexed Ankle Position
points: Wide anterior talar trochlea wedges into mortise
Resistant to inversion or eversion sprain

right.title: Plantarflexed Ankle Position
points: Narrow posterior talus sits in wider mortise
Permits small degree of accessory wobble
Common position for inversion ligament tears

steps.tx: Medially, the ankle joint is anchored by the massive **deltoid ligament**, a fan-shaped ligament consisting of superficial and deep components attached to the medial malleolus. The superficial layer spans to the navicular, calcaneus (sustentaculum tali), and talus, while the deep layer attaches directly to the medial non-articular talar body.
steps.say: Medially, the ankle joint is reinforced by the deltoid ligament attached to the medial malleolus. Its superficial fibers attach to the navicular, sustentaculum tali, and talus, while deep fibers bind to the medial talus.

rows: Resists foot eversion; supports spring ligament
Resists valgus tilting of the calcaneus
Strongest component; prevents lateral talar shift

steps.tx: Because the deltoid ligament is exceedingly strong, severe eversion violence usually avulses the medial malleolus rather than tearing the ligament. Conversely, lateral ligament injury from hyperinversion is the most common musculoskeletal injury, specifically rupturing the **anterior talofibular ligament** (ATFL), followed by the calcaneofibular ligament in severe sprains.
steps.say: Because the deltoid ligament is exceptionally tough, severe eversion fractures the medial malleolus instead of tearing the ligament. In contrast, sudden inversion sprains most commonly tear the anterior talofibular ligament.

steps.tx: Rigid unyielding fascial envelopes make the leg the most frequent site of acute **compartment syndrome**. Traumatic tibial shaft fractures elevate intracompartmental tissue pressure above thirty millimetres of mercury, collapsing capillaries and inducing irreversible muscle necrosis within six hours unless emergency fasciotomy unroofs all four leg compartments.
steps.say: Rigid fascial walls make the leg the prime site for acute compartment syndrome. Tibial fractures can raise tissue pressure above capillary perfusion thresholds, causing muscle necrosis unless emergency decompressive fasciotomy is performed.

vis.title: Cascade of Acute Leg Compartment Syndrome

nodes.label: Tibial Fracture or Crush Trauma Causes Intracompartmental Bleeding
Tissue Pressure Exceeds Capillary Perfusion Pressure (30 mmHg)
Severe Pain Out of Proportion and Pain on Passive Stretch

steps.tx: Behind and below the medial malleolus lies the **tarsal tunnel**, roofed by the flexor retinaculum extending from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus. Four structures pass through this tunnel from anterior to posterior (Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry): Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, posterior tibial Artery and Vein, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus.
steps.say: The tarsal tunnel lies behind the medial malleolus under the flexor retinaculum. Transmitted structures follow the classic mnemonic: tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, posterior tibial vessels, tibial nerve, and flexor hallucis longus.

rows: Palpation site for posterior tibial pulse
Splits into medial and lateral plantar

steps.tx: Compression of the tibial nerve within the tarsal tunnel causes tarsal tunnel syndrome, characterized by burning pain, paresthesias, and numbness across the sole and plantar surfaces of the toes. Symptoms are worsened by prolonged standing, and percussion behind the medial malleolus produces a diagnostic **Tinel sign** radiating into the plantar foot.
steps.say: Entrapment of the tibial nerve inside the tarsal tunnel produces tarsal tunnel syndrome. Patients experience burning sole pain and numbness that worsen with walking, elicited by Tinel percussion behind the medial malleolus.

left.title: Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome
points: Numbness and burning over entire sole

steps.tx: Terminal bifurcation of the tibial nerve within the tarsal tunnel gives rise to the medial and lateral plantar nerves, accompanied by the medial and lateral plantar arteries. These structures pass deep to the abductor hallucis muscle to enter the four muscular layers of the **plantar aspect** of the foot, orchestrating foot propulsion.
steps.say: Inside the tarsal tunnel, the tibial nerve splits into medial and lateral plantar nerves. Passing under abductor hallucis, they enter the four muscle layers of the sole to control intrinsic foot biomechanics.

vis.alt: Course and division of medial and lateral plantar nerves across the four layers of the sole
vis.caption: Bifurcation of the tibial nerve into medial and lateral plantar nerves within the sole. [Credit: StewardMD]
